chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Hafs, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), said:

I asked him about a group of people who had springs in a land, close to one another. A man intended to make his spring lower than its original position. If he did so, some of the remaining springs would be harmed, while others would not be harmed due to the solidity of the land.

He said: He said, 'Whatever is in a solid place will not be harmed, and whatever is in soft, flat land will be harmed. And if he offers his neighbor to place his spring at the same level and measurement, he said, 'If they both agree, there is no harm.' And he said, 'There should be a distance of one thousand cubits between the two springs.'
ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for water rights and neighborly damages in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* elucidates the principle of *al-darar* (harm) in Islamic jurisprudence, distinguishing between physical damage in soft soil versus solid ground to determine liability for altering water sources. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on both objective physical consequences and subjective mutual consent (*taradhi*) in neighborly relations, while establishing a standard distance of one thousand cubits to prevent interference. This ruling serves as a foundational text for water rights (*haqq al-shirbah*) and property damage in urban and rural contexts.
